The year is 1563 and you are born in London,
in a narrow house on Cheapside, the busiest street in the city.
Your home sits above your father’s shop,
and it smells of hot tallow, beeswax,
and the smoke of a hundred candles. Your father is a chandler.
He makes candles for churches, taverns, and the houses of the rich.
He is a quiet,
careful man with burn scars on his fingers and
a belief that honest work will always be enough.
Your mother is a seamstress.
She is sharp, ambitious, and she has one dream for her daughter.
A better life than hers.
You arrive one year after the Queen of England almost dies.
In 1562, Queen Elizabeth the First catches smallpox.
She survives, but the disease leaves scars across her face.
So the Queen does what any queen would do. She covers them.
With a thick, perfect layer of white paint.
And within a few years,
every woman in England wants to look exactly like her.
You don’t know any of this yet.
You’re too busy being a child.
By age 5, you’re running up and down Cheapside,
chasing dogs and stealing candle ends from your father’s bench.
By age 8, you can climb the churchyard wall faster
than any boy on the street.
You spend every hour you can outside, in the sun,
laughing so loudly that the neighbours lean out
of their windows to tell you to hush.
And the sun leaves its mark on you. Freckles. Dozens of them.
Across your nose, your cheeks, your arms.
You love them. Your father calls them your sun kisses.
Some evenings he lets you sit at his
workbench and dip wicks into the hot tallow,
and he counts the freckles on your nose while the candles cool.
He always loses count around forty and has to start again.
You think it’s the funniest thing in the world.
Your mother does not love them.
To her, freckles are a disaster.
In Elizabethan England, the most beautiful skin is pale. White as milk.
White as the Queen.
A pale face tells the world that you’re a lady,
that you never have to work outdoors like a peasant.
Freckles tell the world the opposite.
So every night,
your mother sits you on a stool by the fire
and scrubs your face with lemon juice and buttermilk. It stings.
It doesn’t work. She tries again.
And every morning, as she ties your bonnet tight against the sun,
she says the same thing.
Keep your face out of the sun, sweetheart.
Your face is your fortune.
You don’t really understand what that means.
You will.
Years pass, and in 1579, you turn 16.
One afternoon, a steward from a great house on the Strand comes
into the shop to order candles for his mistress,
the Countess of Ashby. While your father writes up the order,
the steward watches you sewing in the corner. Neat stitches. Quiet hands.
He mentions that the Countess needs a new chamber maid.
Someone young, careful, and well-mannered.
Your mother’s eyes light up like a church on Christmas Eve.
Within a week, you’re packed and gone.
The first month is disorienting in the best possible way.
The Countess’s house is enormous, with gardens running down to the Thames,
glass in every window, and more candles burning in one night
than your father sells in a month.
You eat white bread and roast meat.
You sleep in a real bed,
shared with only one other maid instead of three sisters.
The Countess gives you her old gowns, cut down to fit you.
Silk. Actual silk.
You write home to tell your mother.
You can practically hear her crying with joy through the paper.
Then, on your second week,
the Countess calls you to her dressing table.
She’s sitting in front of a large silver mirror,
and she’s covered in white. Her face. Her neck. Her chest.
A smooth, flawless, ghostly white, like a statue carved from marble.
Her cheeks are painted a bright rosy red.
Her lips are red too.
Her eyebrows have been plucked into thin, perfect arches,
and her hairline has been plucked back, high up her forehead,
to make it look smooth and noble.
She looks at you in the mirror. She looks at your freckles.
And she sighs.
That will never do, she says.
That evening, for the first time in your life, you’re painted.
The Countess’s older maid, a woman called Joan, does it.
Joan is about thirty, round-faced and sharp-tongued, from a farm in Kent,
with a laugh like a goose and absolutely no respect for anyone,
including the Countess, when the Countess isn’t listening.
She sits you down and opens a little pot of white paste.
She tells you it’s called Venetian ceruse.
The finest face paint in the world.
Imported from Venice, the most fashionable city in Europe.
It costs more than your father earns in a month.
She dips a soft brush into the pot
and paints it across your face in long, smooth strokes.
It’s cold and slightly greasy. It smells faintly of vinegar.
Then she holds up the mirror.
Your freckles are gone.
All of them. Every single sun kiss.
In their place is a smooth, white, perfect face. A lady’s face.
You look like a stranger. You look like the Queen.
You can’t stop staring.
The next morning, the Countess’s guests compliment you at breakfast.
A lady asks who your family are.
Another asks where you found such a delicate complexion.
The cook gives you an extra slice of pie.
For the first time in your life, you feel beautiful.
You decide that whoever invented Venetian ceruse was a genius.
You find out what’s actually in it a month later,
when you’re sent to collect a fresh pot from the apothecary.
He’s an old man with bad breath
and a workshop full of strange bottles. He explains how it’s made,
as proudly as if he invented it himself.
You take sheets of lead.
You hang them over vinegar in a sealed pot,
and bury the pot in horse dung for weeks,
so the heat makes the vinegar fumes eat into the metal.
The lead turns into a white, crumbly crust.
You scrape it off, grind it into powder,
and mix it into a paste.
White lead. That’s what you’re painting on your face.
You ask the apothecary if it’s safe.
He laughs and asks if the Queen looks dead to you.
You don’t ask again.
There’s more, of course. Much more.
Every morning, Joan teaches you the full routine.
First, wash your face with rosewater.
Then, to remove any blemishes or freckles that might show through,
dab them with a lotion made from mercury. It burns like fire.
It peels the top layer of skin right off. That’s the point.
Then the ceruse.
Then a thin glaze of egg white over the top,
to make it shine like porcelain and
stop it cracking when you smile.
Then rouge for the cheeks and lips,
made from a bright red powder called vermilion.
Which is also, Joan mentions, made from mercury.
And finally, for special occasions,
a drop of juice from the deadly nightshade plant in each eye.
Belladonna. It makes your pupils huge, dark, and mysterious.
It also makes your vision blurry for hours,
and if you use too much, it can stop your heart.
The first time you try the belladonna,
for the Countess’s Twelfth Night feast,
the whole hall turns into a soft golden blur.
You walk straight into a pillar. Then into the steward.
Then down two steps you never saw.
The guests think you’ve had too much wine.
Joan has to lead you around by the elbow all night,
whispering directions in your ear like a ship’s pilot.
You learn all of this in your first year.
You learn it well.
Joan becomes your favourite person in the house.
She’s has opinions on everything. She thinks the plucked hairlines make the
court ladies look like boiled eggs.
She thinks the Countess’s new perfume smells like
a cat that’s been dipped in rosewater.
And one night, when she’s taking off her own paint,
she admits something she’s never told anyone.
She hates the mercury. It hurts too much.
So she’s stopped using it. She just uses more ceruse instead,
a thicker layer to cover whatever’s underneath.
You notice that her paint has been
getting thicker for a while now.
Years pass. You stop being the new girl. By 1585, you’re 22,
and you’re the one teaching the younger maids how to paint.
Your hands are steady. Your strokes are perfect.
The Countess calls you her artist.
One spring, a new girl arrives from the country.
Her name is Alice.
She’s fifteen, nervous, and covered in freckles, dozens of them,
across her nose and cheeks.
She stands in front of the Countess’s mirror,
and the Countess looks at her, and sighs.
And you hear your own voice say it. That will never do.
You paint her that evening. Long, smooth strokes.
When you hold up the mirror, she gasps, the way you did.
You tell yourself you’ve given her a gift.
But something is happening to Joan.
It starts with her hair. When you brush it at night,
more of it stays in the brush.
She starts wearing her caps lower. Then her teeth.
One of them goes black. Then another.
She stops smiling with her mouth open.
Then the headaches come.
Terrible ones, that leave her lying in a dark room for days.
She gets tired easily. Her hands shake when she holds the brush.
Some days, she forgets your name. Some days, she forgets her own.
And the skin underneath her paint. You see it one night,
when she’s too exhausted to wash her
face alone and lets you do it.
Under the white mask, her real skin is grey. Not pale. Grey.
Rough and blotchy and scarred,
like old parchment left out in the rain.
You don’t say anything. You just wash her face gently and
paint it again in the morning.
Joan catches you looking.
She tells you not to worry, that it’s only the winter air,
that she’s tougher than a Kentish turnip.
Then she does her impression of the Countess sneezing,
and you both laugh, and for one evening,
you let yourself believe her.
The Countess’s physician comes.
He says Joan suffers from an excess of melancholy. Bad humours.
He bleeds her. It doesn’t help.
In the winter of 1587, Joan dies. She’s 38 years old.
You’re the one who prepares her body for burial.
And when you’ve washed the last of the paint from her face,
you look down and realize you can’t
remember what she really looked like.
In eight years, you never saw her without it.
You stand in the dark for a long time.
They bury her in the corner of a churchyard near the river.
The Countess doesn’t attend. She has a supper that evening,
and she needs you there to do her face.
Then you go to your own room,
sit down at your little mirror, and slowly wash your own face.
And underneath, for the first time, you see it.
Small grey patches across your cheeks.
Little pits and scars where the mercury burned too deep.
The skin around your mouth rough and thin.
Your freckles are long gone. What replaced them is worse.
Something cold settles in your stomach.
You understand, finally, what’s been happening. It’s the paint.
The paint is ruining the skin.
And the only way to hide the ruined skin is more paint.
Which ruins more skin. Which needs more paint.
You think about stopping. You really do.
But without the paint, you’d be a grey,
scarred maid with a ruined face.
The Countess would dismiss you by the end of the week.
Your mother would die of shame. And you would have nothing.
So in the morning, you pick up the brush.
That summer, your mother comes to visit.
She hasn’t seen you in years.
When you walk into the kitchen in your
silk gown and your perfect white face, she bursts into tears.
She holds your painted cheeks in her rough seamstress hands
and tells you you look like a real lady.
Like the Queen herself. She says she always knew it.
You smile with your lips closed. You don’t tell her what’s underneath.
You couldn’t bear to.
Your face is your fortune.
Years pass. The paint gets thicker. Your hair thins.
One of your back teeth turns black,
and you learn to smile with your lips closed,
the way Joan did. Some mornings, your hands shake.
Some nights, the headaches are so bad
you see colours that aren’t there.
The Countess is suffering too.
Her paint is now so thick it cracks when she talks.
She’s started covering her ruined skin with even more ceruse,
and her hair is so thin she wears a wig.
Everyone at court does. Nobody mentions it. Nobody would dare.
Some mornings, the Countess sits at her mirror for three
hours before she’s ready to be seen.
She has you add layer after layer,
until her face looks less like skin
and more like a plastered wall. Then she smiles at her reflection,
and the paint cracks at the corners of her mouth,
and you start all over again.
In the winter of 1600,
the Countess takes you with her to the royal palace at Whitehall.
For the first time in your life, you see the Queen.
She’s 67 years old.
She’s sitting on a throne under a canopy of gold,
in a dress covered in pearls.
And her face is the whitest thing in the room.
Thicker paint than you’ve ever seen. A mask, really.
Her hair is a bright orange wig.
Her teeth, when she speaks, are black.
The servants whisper that the Queen hasn’t allowed
a true mirror near her in years.
That she can’t bear to see what’s underneath.
You look at her.
And for a moment, you swear she looks right back at you.
Two painted faces,
staring at each other across a room full of candles.
Your father might have made those candles.
Three years later, in March 1603, the Queen dies at Richmond Palace.
She’s 69. They say she spent her last days
sitting on cushions on the floor,
refusing to eat, refusing to sleep, staring at nothing.
Nobody is quite sure what killed her.
Some later historians will wonder whether decades
of lead paint played a part.
You are 40 now. You’ve buried Joan. You’ve buried the Countess,
who died of what the physician called a wasting fever,
though you saw her face and knew better.
You live in a small rented room near
Cheapside with what little money you’ve saved,
and you paint your face every morning out of habit,
even though no one’s left to see it.
And one morning, in the spring, you don’t.
You don’t know why that day. Maybe you’re just tired.
You wash your face, look at the grey,
scarred skin in the mirror, and you put the brush down.
Then you take off your cap, open the door,
and step out into the sun.
The street is noisy and bright. Someone is selling oranges.
A dog runs past you. Children are climbing the churchyard wall.
You turn your face up, close your eyes,
and feel the warmth on your ruined cheeks.
For the first time in twenty-four years,
your face is just a face.
A few months later, a fever takes you.
The doctor writes melancholy and weakness of the blood. Nobody writes lead.
You’re 40 years old.
